Date: 2026-09-14
Time: 15:00 - 15:52 UTC

Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Lee (Nebula CTO), Sarah Gomez (Nebula SRE), Jason Park (Nebula Product), Elena Ruiz (Nebula Security)
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs for Nebula Finance. Focus on debugging flows, per-request traces, sampling/retention tradeoffs, linking traces to request IDs and model variants, and next steps for POC. Customer concerned about data residency, retention cost, SSO/RBAC, and ability to search request logs by X-Request-ID and model rollout tags.
topics: Linking traces to model variants and fallback policies
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna walk through the Redwood Console tracing and request logs piece. Priya and I will show the flows and answer questions.
[00:10] Mark: Great, thanks. We want to see how quickly we can triage timeouts and bad outputs, and how this ties back to model versions.
[00:18] Priya: Perfect. Quick agenda — tracing timeline, request-log search, error-analysis panel, linking to model rollouts, and sampling/retention controls.
[00:28] Sarah: For us latency spikes are the biggest pain, also noisy retries from our web tier. We need per-request token timing ideally.
[00:35] Priya: Yes, we surface per-token and per-stage timings in the trace. So you can see the client->gateway, routing, model decode, and post-processing latencies. Note: timestamps are approximate, transcription may miss some technical names.
[00:50] Alex: I'm sharing screen — here's the trace view. You can search by trace id or X-Request-ID header — we recommend propagating X-Request-ID from your front end.
[01:05] Jason: Does Redwood pick up headers automatically or we need to pass them in the API?
[01:09] Priya: You pass them. If you include request_id in metadata, it becomes a first-class indexed field. We also auto-attach model_variant and region tags.
[01:20] Sarah: How long do traces stay? We can't keep full payloads for more than 30 days without encrypting differently.
[01:27] Alex: Default retention is 90 days at full fidelity for hosted customers, but you can configure shorter retention or sample traces. For regulated customers we support private deployment and custom retention via Redwood Private — also KMS-backed encryption for at-rest fields.
[01:42] Elena: On encryption, can we get a customer-managed key (HSM/KMS)?
[01:46] Priya: Yes, for Private we support customer-managed KMS. For Dedicated there's an option too; we'll include the exact matrix in the security pack.
[01:56] Mark: Show us an example error analysis flow — how do we go from an error rate spike to the root cause?
[02:03] Priya: Right — in the console you can go to the model route metrics, select an interval, see error rate percent, then jump to the request-log table filtered to only errors. From any request row you can open the trace timeline and jump into the raw request/response JSON.
[02:20] Alex: I'll filter to a 10-minute window where we saw retries — see the spike here. Click 'Jump to sample requests' — these are the top N representative errors by frequency and latency.
[02:33] Sarah: How do you pick representative requests? Sometimes outliers skew the view.
[02:37] Priya: We bucket by error type and then pick median-latency sample per bucket to avoid outliers; you can also sort by longest tail or furthest from SLO.
[02:49] Jason: Can we tag traces with deployment metadata? We run canary rollouts and need to correlate errors with specific model hashes.
[02:56] Priya: Absolutely — the console ingests model_version, commit_hash, and rollout_tag. If you call the API with model: 'redwood/gptx-v2-canary' that tag shows up. Also automatic fallback events are recorded so you can see when a request was routed to a cheaper model due to capacity.
[03:15] Mark: Is the request log query language SQL-like? We have existing tooling for logs.
[03:20] Alex: It's a simple filter UI plus a query bar that supports boolean expressions and dot notation for nested JSON. Example: status = "error" AND metadata.request_id = "abc-123". We can export search results as CSV or JSON into S3.
[03:36] Elena: Audit logs — who viewed traces? We need granular audit trails for compliance.
[03:41] Priya: We record user actions in audit logs: view, export, share. RBAC controls limit who can see PII fields and full payloads. We'll attach the RBAC matrix in the security pack.
[03:54] Sarah: What about cost — storing full request bodies gets expensive. Any best practices?
[03:59] Alex: Common pattern: store full payloads for a short window (7-30 days), keep indexed metadata longer, and use sampled traces for long-term trend analysis. Redwood Optimize can recommend sampling rates based on request distribution.
[04:12] Mark: For POC we'd like 7-day full fidelity and 90-day metadata, can Redwood support that?
[04:18] Priya: Yes, that's a common config. If you go Dedicated or Private we can also offer custom retention policies.
[04:26] Jason: Debugging flow — can we replay requests into a sandboxed model variant?
[04:30] Priya: You can replay request payloads to a debug endpoint in a sandbox tenant. We strip credentials by default and you can opt in to include more context. Replays are rate-limited and isolated to avoid tampering.
[04:43] Alex: Also we store condensed diffs for regenerations — so you can see prompt + delta tokens between runs, useful for regression analysis.
[04:52] Sarah: How are traces correlated across microservices? We have internal trace IDs and then the Redwood request id.
[04:57] Priya: If you propagate your trace id via a header, we attach it to the Redwood trace and link via a join_key. The console shows external trace links so you can click through to your tracing system if you have cross-service instrumentation.
[05:12] Mark: Any limits on query throughput for logs? We run a few thousand searches during incident response windows.
[05:18] Alex: There are query rate limits on the UI for hosted tiers to protect platform stability; Dedicated customers get higher quotas and can request temporary emergency boosts. We'll include exact quotas in the offer.
[05:30] Jason: Show me the request details pane — I want to see prompt, model, token counts, decoding settings, and the KV cache hit/miss info.
[05:39] Priya: Opening a request — here's the header with model, route, region, embed/seq length, then the trace timeline, then the raw JSON. Note the token counts and decoding mode. KV cache events are shown as a separate swimlane.
[05:55] Sarah: Is the data redaction configurable? We need to remove PII before it's stored.
[05:59] Priya: Yes — you can configure server-side scrubbing rules to redact fields or apply a transform before ingestion. There's a policy UI and a webhook to approve flagged items.
[06:12] Alex: Quick demo of an error: here's a request with an "invalid_token" response from our tokenizer. Jump to the error analysis panel — it surfaces stack traces from the runtime and correlated config changes (e.g., recent quantization profile change).
[06:28] Mark: That helps. Do you integrate with PagerDuty or Slack for alerting?
[06:33] Priya: Yes, we have alerting hooks and prebuilt integrations for PagerDuty, Slack, and Datadog. You can base alerts on trace-level metrics or aggregated error rates.
[06:44] Jason: We use internal metrics stack; can we send events via webhook to our ingest pipeline?
[06:48] Alex: Webhooks and Kafka connectors are supported for streaming request logs and traces to your platform.
[06:55] Elena: About data residency — our legal needs EU-only hosting for logs.
[06:59] Priya: We have EU regions and can pin customer data to the region. For Private on-prem installs you keep everything behind your VPC. We'll document the region map in the security pack.
[07:12] Mark: Ok next, operationalizing — we'd like a runbook example for an SLO breach.
[07:16] Alex: We'll provide a runbook template: triage via console, filter high-latency traces, isolate model variant, run replay on sample requests, then apply temporary routing to a higher-capacity variant. We'll attach a sample runbook to the follow-up.
[07:31] Sarah: One more: can we correlate regressions to prompt sets / evals?
[07:36] Priya: Redwood Optimize ties eval sets to routes — when a regression hits a threshold, it flags the eval and can auto-open an alert. You can link the failing prompts directly from a trace.
[07:48] Mark: Great. Any known caveats with quantized models and tracing? Sometimes kernel-level failures are hard to interpret.
[07:55] Priya: True — we try to surface hardware and kernel errors in the trace metadata, but debugging low-level kernel OOMs sometimes requires logs from the Dedicated host. For those cases we coordinate with infra and can run a dedicated capture.
[08:10] Alex: Recap and next steps: we'll send the security pack + RBAC matrix, provision a demo tenant, ingest the 24h request dump, and schedule the POC benchmark.
[08:20] Mark: Sounds good. Thanks both.
[08:22] Jason: Quick note — can you include an example of the query used to find requests that hit fallback?
[08:27] Priya: Example query: routing.fallback = true AND model_variant : "canary" AND status = "ok". We'll add a few canned queries in the tenant.
[08:38] Elena: Thanks.
[08:40] Alex: We'll follow up in email with the items. End of walk-through.
[08:44] [call ends]
